rationale: A wins because it does the newsroom work: it turns the supplied facts into testable desks and proof gates, especially "Proof it needs: the actual durability test methodology and results." B has sharp instincts, but it keeps stepping over the evidence with lines like "Allbirds Quietly Dropped 'Eco-Friendly' as Its Main Pitch," which the update never says. That is how a decent angle set gets itself escorted out of the editor's office.
gaps_in_A: "That's a company publicly conceding its signature product had a durability problem" overstates the supplied fact. The update says the new blend is more durable, not that Allbirds confessed a defect.
"A DTC pioneer that spent a decade avoiding wholesale" imports a decade-long channel history not supplied in the update.
"The sustainable-shoe brand that had to prove its shoes last" is a good thesis, but it leans on sustainability and low-carbon positioning the update only implies through natural materials.
The two durability angles are close cousins; A admits this with "If the founder can't or won't say...these collapse," but still keeps both live.
gaps_in_B: "Allbirds Quietly Dropped 'Eco-Friendly' as Its Main Pitch" is an invented marketing shift. The update never says Allbirds dropped eco-friendly messaging.
"For a Brand Built on Cutting Out Middlemen, That's a Concession" rests on a DTC origin story not provided in the supplied facts.
Refusing "Allbirds' sugarcane-wool blend is a materials innovation story" throws away a real materials/durability-testing desk. Call it unproven, not dead.
The next step says "meanest-editor" and calls angles "ready to draft once the partner name is confirmed"; the real next step is journalist fit-check plus proof, especially durability data.
